title: Adding CSS to HTML 🔗
description: Master inline, internal, and external stylesheets and learn which to use when.

slides.title: Three Ways to Apply CSS 🧩
slides.content:
# Inline, Internal, External

1. **Inline** – using the `style` attribute directly on an HTML element.
2. **Internal** – a `<style>` block inside the HTML `<head>`.
3. **External** – a separate `.css` file linked via `<link>`.

Each has its place, but external is the industry standard for maintainability.

slides.title: External Stylesheets (Best Practice) 🏆
slides.content:
# The `<link>` Element

An external CSS file is a plain text file with a `.css` extension. Link it in `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
```
Advantages:
- Separation of concerns (HTML vs CSS).
- Cached by the browser, improving load times.
- Reusable across multiple pages.
- Easier to maintain and scale.

quizData.question: Which method links an external CSS file?
quizData.explanation: The `<link>` tag with `rel="stylesheet"` is the standard way to load external CSS.

slides.title: Order Matters: Overriding Styles 📊
slides.content:
# Which Style Wins?

When multiple styles target the same element, the order of specificity and source decides. Inline beats internal/external (unless `!important`). Among stylesheets, the one that loads last overrides previous ones.

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="reset.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="main.css">
```
`main.css` can override rules from `reset.css`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Organise Your Stylesheets

For large projects, split CSS into multiple files (e.g., `layout.css`, `typography.css`, `components.css`). Use a build tool to combine them for production.
